items.passage: Executives make proclamations; employees deal with implementation. It’s easy to feel optimistic about AI when your relationship to it is strategic rather than operational. The messy details of actually making AI work—prompt engineering, data cleanup, training it on proprietary information, error correction, the workflow integration—fall to the people doing the actual work. Things look and feel much better when you aren’t in the weeds.

source_piece.title: Executives and Employees Disagree on How Much Time AI Saves. Here's Why.

hook.headline: Companies risk losing their most AI-savvy employees while leaving majority behind: PwC

platform_cuts.linkedin:
PwC surveyed 49,364 workers across 48 countries and regions. AI use at work is rising, but access to learning resources fell from 59% last year to 51%. Among the 56% PwC calls the "engine room" of the workforce, only two in five say they have the learning resources they need.

Executives make proclamations; employees deal with implementation. It’s easy to feel optimistic about AI when your relationship to it is strategic rather than operational. The messy details of actually making AI work—prompt engineering, data cleanup, training it on proprietary information, error correction, the workflow integration—fall to the people doing the actual work.

Things look and feel much better when you aren’t in the weeds. If you want AI gains across the company, invest in the workers doing the implementation.

The organizations figuring this out have an AI lead who is AI-native, or close to it, overseeing usage across the company. When AI lives inside the legacy IT department, you get process and compliance. Experimentation and cost discipline come from giving it its own home.
